newsitem.title: UK: Labour still doubts it can force early UK polls.
newsitem.headline: Labour still doubts it can force early UK polls.

text.p: The death of a Conservative MP on Thursday put Prime Minister John Major into a minority in the British parliament but is unlikely to boost Labour's chances of forcing an early election, a senior Labour strategist said.

The Labour Party official said the death of Iain Mills would be a psychological blow to the Conservatives and would mean the ruling party could afford less than ever to lower its guard in late-night votes.

"But the fact is we have no chance of defeating the government unless the Ulster Unionists vote against them -- and there's no sign that they'll do that. So I don't think it will make that much difference," the strategist told Reuters.
Major also signalled that it would be business as usual.
"His (Major's) thoughts are that the government will remain the government and business will carry on as he intends it should," an aide said.

Labour's chief whip, Donald Dewar, has said Labour would call a vote of no-confidence if it saw a genuine prospect of toppling the government and thus advancing the general election, which must be held by May 22.
But Dewar said as recently as Monday that, as a realist, he thought the odds were that Major would be able to soldier on until he chose to call the election.

For a vote of confidence to succeed, Labour would not only have to muster all its MPs -- at least one of whom is seriously ill -- but also persuade every member of all other opposition parties, including the Ulster Unionists, to vote with it.
The Conservatives now have 322 MPs and the opposition parties have 323.
Mills, MP for Meriden in central England, had a 14,699 majority at the 1992 election. He was 56 and made the headlines last April when he was arrested for drunkenness and released with a warning.
